feed.subtitle: Real cases from around the world, three times a week, across every Wits AHEAD project.

entry.title: Logistic regression and random forest both reach above 90 per cent accuracy in a Lithuanian dropout study (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A researcher at Vilnius Gediminas Technical University compared six machine-learning models, logistic regression, support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, k-nearest neighbours and a neural network, on an open-access dataset of 4,424 student records with 36 attributes. Logistic regression and random forest performed best, reaching accuracy above 90 per cent and a ROC AUC of up to 0.96, with first and second semester academic performance, tuition fee payment status, outstanding debt, scholarship status, age at enrolment and study programme the most significant risk factors.

Why it matters here: The study's comparison of simple, interpretable models such as logistic regression against more complex ones, on routinely collected enrolment and fee data rather than bespoke instruments, gives PASS a benchmark for how far an interpretable baseline model can go before the Wits-Emory team turns to more complex methods, and its risk-factor list (fees, scholarships, age at enrolment) is a useful checklist against the Business Intelligence Services data.

Mincevičius, New Trends in Computer Sciences, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access, confirmed via DOI resolution and the publisher's own article page.

entry.title: An opinion piece argues Belgium's tighter student visa rules fall heaviest on African applicants (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
An opinion piece in The Brussels Times argues that Belgium's tightened rules for non-EU students, which require bachelor's students to accumulate 100 credits by the end of their third year, raise the required proof of funds to 1,050 euro a month and allow fees of up to 17,500 euro a year at some institutions, filter students by wealth rather than merit. It reports more than 2,615 student visa rejections in the preceding cycle, falling heavily on applicants from Cameroon and Morocco, and calls for Belgium to replace brain-drain fears with a brain-circulation model of trade-aligned visa pathways, diaspora scholarships and post-study search years.

Why it matters here: As a mobility scheme that depends on African partner universities and on African students and staff being able to obtain visas, the Wits and Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ project has a direct stake in this kind of evidence on how tightening student visa rules can disproportionately affect African applicants elsewhere in Europe, and in the brain-circulation alternative the piece proposes.

Nweke, The Brussels Times, 2026 · Opinion article in an established Belgian English-language news outlet, confirmed by fetching the page.

entry.title: An enterprise system switch gives a Caribbean campus one-click visibility into which students have stopped returning (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The University of the West Indies Five Islands Campus in Antigua moved to an Ellucian Banner enterprise system in July 2025, covering student registration, finance, accounts receivable, data migration and reporting and analytics. Campus Registrar Dr Camille Samuel reported that the platform gives her team one-click visibility into student progress and retention, letting staff identify students who have not returned and intervene early.

Why it matters here: This is a small Caribbean campus choosing an off-the-shelf enterprise system, rather than a bespoke model, to get early-alert visibility, which is a relevant contrast for PASS as the Wits-Emory team weighs a purpose-built predictive model against the reporting tools the University's Business Intelligence Services already runs.

Antigua News, 2026 · News report, Antigua News, confirmed by fetching the published article.

entry.title: Two Tanzanian teacher educators complete a staff mobility placement at a Finnish university (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Two teacher educators from the Dar es Salaam University College of Education in Tanzania spent a two-week staff mobility placement at the University of Eastern Finland from 13 to 27 March 2026, hosted jointly with the Finnish National Agency for Education. The visit, held under the Future Teachers in East Africa (FUTE) project, included teaching, school visits and joint curriculum work, and continued a longer-term partnership on teacher education between the two institutions.

Why it matters here: A short, reciprocal staff placement built around joint curriculum work and school visits, rather than a one-off conference trip, offers a concrete format for the shorter staff exchanges envisaged under the Wits and Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ project, and the sustained Finland-Tanzania partnership behind it is a further point of comparison for how the Wits School of Education and Aix-Marseille's INSPE might deepen their own exchange over successive mobility rounds.

University of Eastern Finland, School of Applied Educational Science and Teacher Education, 2026 · Institutional news item, University of Eastern Finland, confirmed by fetching the page.

entry.title: A neural network outperforms eight other models in predicting dropout at Côte d'Ivoire's virtual university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Virtual University of Côte d'Ivoire compared nine machine-learning and deep-learning models on 9,881 student records with 14 features. A neural network performed best, with an F1 score of 0.9888 and accuracy of 0.9930, ahead of gradient boosting, the best traditional machine-learning model, at an F1 score of 0.9406 and accuracy of 0.9641.

Why it matters here: A fully online, Francophone West African university reaching this scale of comparison, nine models on nearly 10,000 records, shows PASS what a resource-constrained, fully digital institution can build from its own enrolment data, and the gap between the neural network and the simpler gradient-boosting model is a useful caution for the Wits-Emory team on how much complexity the Business Intelligence Services data can justify.

Kone and Achi, International Journal of Advanced Research, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Advanced Research), confirmed via DOI resolution to the publisher's page and cross-checked against the authors' Zenodo deposit of the same study.

entry.title: A mixed-methods study measures gains from Kahoot-based gamification in aircraft maintenance training (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A study at the Philippine State College of Aeronautics assessed 120 participants in Aircraft Maintenance Technology education using Kahoot-based gamification, combining quantitative surveys, pre- and post-assessments and qualitative interviews with students and instructors. The study reports statistically significant gains after the gamified intervention: engagement up by 43.8 per cent, motivation by 55.2 per cent, knowledge retention by 41.2 per cent and practical skills by 51.6 per cent. It also names internet connectivity, time constraints and question-format limitations as practical challenges, and recommends blending gamification with hands-on training and technologies such as augmented and virtual reality.

Why it matters here: The size of the measured gains across engagement, retention and practical skills gives the Wits project a concrete benchmark for what a well-run Kahoot-style quiz layer can add on top of hands-on technical training, and its identified barriers, connectivity, time and question format, are exactly the practical constraints the co-design workshops with metallurgical engineering students will need to plan around.

Dela Peña, Research in Learning Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Research in Learning Technology (Association for Learning Technology), open access, confirmed via DOI resolution.

entry.title: ChemChallenge, an open-source video game for teaching thermodynamics to chemical engineering undergraduates (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
An associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong built ChemChallenge, described as the first video game with in-game currency and non-linear gameplay rather than a quiz format, to help undergraduates studying chemistry and chemical engineering practise thermodynamics and thermochemistry by designing reaction equations for spontaneous reactions. The game's reward system is built on thermodynamic principles, it is freeware distributed under the GNU General Public License 3.0 with its source code on GitHub, and colleagues at the university tested it and gave feedback before release. The author is seeking to integrate it into a physical chemistry course.

Why it matters here: A free, open-source game whose scoring is itself built from the underlying thermodynamics, rather than an unrelated points system, is a kit the Wits project could trial or adapt directly for teaching phase transformations and structure-property relationships, and its open licence means the co-design workshops could modify it rather than build a game from scratch.

Savateev, Springer Nature Research Communities ('Behind the Paper'), 2025 · Author's own account on Springer Nature's 'Behind the Paper' research-communities platform, describing a game whose preprint and source code are both publicly posted; read directly, not independently peer-reviewed.

entry.title: A virtual reality serious game trialled with mining engineering postgraduates to teach hazard detection (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Pretoria built a virtual reality serious game to teach hazard detection in mines and tested it with eleven students who had completed mining engineering studies at a public South African university and had prior experience of an active mining site. The study used an action research design, with a pre-survey, one hour of gameplay, a post-survey and focus groups, to examine how 'meaningful choice' design, choices that genuinely affect the game's outcome, shaped the learning experience. Participants reported that meaningful choices, including a realistic equipment system and random hazard generation, made the experience more engaging and personally adapted to their own strengths, though some wanted starker consequences for poor choices.

Why it matters here: The game's choice-driven design for teaching a hazardous, high-stakes identification task offers the Wits project a worked example of how 'meaningful choice' mechanics, not just points or badges, can be built into a game for a technical engineering subject such as crystallography or phase identification, and its qualitative focus-group method is a close match for the interviews and focus groups already planned for the metallurgical engineering study.

Wong, Bothma and Smith, International Journal of Serious Games, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, International Journal of Serious Games, open access, confirmed via DOI resolution and the publisher's PDF.

entry.title: Five Namibian lecturers' Erasmus exchange in Vienna opens a fully funded semester for ten students (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Five staff members from the University of Namibia's Department of Applied Educational Sciences visited the University College for Teacher Education in Vienna, Austria, in early 2024 under the Erasmus Staff and Student Mobility Programme, coordinated by Dr Enock Simasiku. The visit aimed to strengthen academic collaboration, enhance teacher training and explore joint research, and opened the way for ten University of Namibia students to join a fully funded six-month study programme in Vienna.

Why it matters here: The progression this partnership shows, from a staff visit to a funded six-month student exchange, is a working model of exactly the kind of staged, reciprocal mobility the Wits and Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ KA171 project is building between the Wits School of Education and INSPE, and the specific focus on teacher education makes it a close comparator for assessing how far the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange's own student numbers might grow.

University of Namibia, UNAM Forum, 2024 · Institutional newsletter article, University of Namibia, confirmed by fetching the page.

entry.title: A new EU call funds student and staff mobility across Africa, not to Europe (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The European Commission's Intra-Africa Academic Mobility Scheme, part of the Global Gateway Youth Mobility for Africa flagship, opened its 2026 call on 3 November 2026 with a closing date of 2 February 2027 and a total budget of 24,750,000 euros, giving each successful project up to 1,450,000 euros. Consortia of five to seven higher education institutions, coordinated by a Sub-Saharan African institution with an EU institution as technical partner and covering at least two of three African regions, can apply to fund student, trainee and staff mobility between African universities themselves rather than to Europe. The call explicitly states it is not a scholarship call, and proposals must address Global Gateway priorities such as climate and energy, digital transformation, transport or health.

Why it matters here: This scheme funds mobility entirely within Africa rather than between Africa and Europe, giving the Wits-Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ project a useful contrast and a possible complement: it shows the European Commission itself investing in African-to-African academic mobility, distinct from the KA171 mobility this project runs, and the Wits School of Education could consider it, or partnerships built through it, as a future, Africa-facing addition to its own mobility portfolio.

European Commission, NDICI-Global Europe call text, reproduced by the Research and Innovation Foundation of Cyprus, 2026 · Official government funding-call listing reproducing the European Commission's own Intra-Africa Academic Mobility Scheme call text under NDICI-Global Europe; read directly from the page.

entry.title: A final-year student builds a Streamlit app that predicts Nigerian students' academic outcomes (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A final-year Computer Science student at Godfrey Okoye University in Enugu, Nigeria, followed the CRISP-DM methodology to analyse 3,630 student records across 37 academic, demographic and lifestyle features, then compared five classification algorithms for predicting academic outcomes. The best model, a decision tree classifier, reached 94.21% accuracy, 100% recall and a 92.95% F1-score, and was deployed as an interactive Streamlit web application with visual analytics and model-comparison tools.

Why it matters here: The project turns a predictive model into a usable, interactive dashboard rather than leaving it a one-off analysis, the same step the PASS project will need once its own models move from the Wits School of Education's anonymised data to tools the University's Business Intelligence Services and advisers can act on; the breadth of its 37 features is also a useful benchmark for how far beyond academic records PASS might reach.

Izunwanne, Nelson Chisom, Godfrey Okoye University institutional repository, 2026 · Undergraduate thesis deposited in Godfrey Okoye University's institutional repository, Faculty of Computing and Information Technology; results as reported on the repository record, not independently peer-reviewed.

entry.title: Nigeria sends a record field of Erasmus Mundus scholars to Europe (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The EU Ambassador to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Gautier Mignot, announced at the 2026 Erasmus Mundus Pre-Departure Orientation in Abuja that 163 Nigerians had been admitted to Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's programmes for 2026, with 89 of them receiving fully funded scholarships, up from 81 the previous year. He said Nigeria remains Africa's top country in the programme and ranks among the five highest-sending countries worldwide, alongside Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and the United States.

Why it matters here: Nigeria's rising, fully funded Erasmus Mundus numbers show one African country turning Erasmus+ scholarship routes into Europe into a large and growing pipeline, which gives the Wits-Aix-Marseille project both a point of comparison for how far South Africa's own Erasmus+ numbers still have to grow and a reminder that KA171-funded mobility, which pays for short stays rather than full master's degrees, serves a different purpose from Erasmus Mundus full-scholarship migration.

Fred Ezeh, The Sun (Nigeria), 5 July 2026 · News report of an EU Delegation pre-departure event in Abuja, naming the EU Ambassador's role and quoting him directly; read directly from the page.

entry.title: A digital escape room tested across four engineering degree programmes in project management (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of La Rioja ran a single two-hour session with 54 students across four engineering degrees (Agricultural, Mechanical, Electrical, and Electronic Industrial and Automation Engineering), using a pre-test, a project-management escape room built on the Escapp platform, a post-test and a satisfaction survey. Working in pairs, students solved eight sequential challenges covering time planning, resource allocation, risk analysis, documentation, budgeting and Gantt chart scheduling in a fictional public project. The escape room produced a small but statistically significant overall gain in test scores, a significant improvement for the Electrical Engineering group, and high satisfaction, especially around teamwork, though satisfaction and perceived learning varied significantly between the four programmes.

Why it matters here: The pre-test and post-test design around a single structured escape room session, run across several distinct engineering degrees at once, offers the Wits project a practical model for comparing a crystallography or phase-transformations game against conventional teaching across different student groups, and the finding that satisfaction varied by programme speaks to the co-design workshops already planned to tailor the game specifically to metallurgical engineering students.

Muro-Fraguas, González-Marcos, Sabando-Fraile, Corral-Bobadilla, Navaridas-Nalda, Sainz-García, Múgica-Vidal and Sainz-García, EDULEARN26 Proceedings, 2026 · Conference proceedings, EDULEARN26 (18th International Conference on Education and New Learning Technologies, Palma, Spain, 29 June to 1 July 2026), confirmed via the IATED Digital Library record and DOI resolution.

entry.title: A Spanish materials course gamifies metal identification using AI-assisted group work (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
At the Universitat Politècnica de València, students on the Design Workshop III course for the Bachelor's Degree in Industrial Design Engineering and Product Development received a short briefing on ferrous and non-ferrous metals, then used course materials and AI tools in small groups to plan how to identify metal samples by their properties. In a three-stage gamified activity, groups scored the most bonus points for correct visual identification of colour, surface finish and apparent weight, fewer points for confirming their answer with magnet and scale tests, and received instructor feedback with a final chance to revise incorrect answers. The authors report high participation and motivation and improved understanding of metal properties, technical observation and teamwork, though the published abstract gives no quantitative results.

Why it matters here: This staged, points-based identification game for ferrous and non-ferrous metals, built around visual and physical tests and explicitly combined with AI tools in the planning stage, is a close practical parallel to the Wits project's own interest in gamifying crystallography, phase transformations and structure-property relationships, and its honest gap, participation and motivation reported but no measured scores, is a reminder for the Wits evaluation to keep quantitative outcomes alongside the planned surveys and focus groups.

Garcia-Garcia, Miranda-Pinzon, Vicente-Viñas, Garcia-Sanoguera, Sanchez-Nacher, Gomez-Caturla and Quiles-Carrillo, EDULEARN26 Proceedings, 2026 · Conference proceedings abstract, EDULEARN26 (18th International Conference on Education and New Learning Technologies, Palma, Spain, 29 June to 1 July 2026), confirmed via the IATED Digital Library record and DOI resolution; the abstract reports qualitative outcomes only, with no sample size or quantitative results given.

entry.title: A Spanish university consortium opens an Erasmus+ KA171 traineeship call for Latin American graduates (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Compostela Group of Universities announced its 2025 to 2026 Erasmus+ KA171-HED project (reference 2024-1-ES01-KA171-HED-000239621) on 26 February 2026, offering recent bachelor's and master's graduates from Universidad de Oriente, Universidad Autónoma de Chihuahua and the Corporación para Investigaciones Biológicas a curricular traineeship in Spain. The four participating Spanish universities, Santiago de Compostela, A Coruña, Oviedo and León, offered placements in fields including new and emerging technologies, earth sciences, the environment, renewable energies, social responsibility and international politics, with traineeships running between May and December 2026 and designed to include applicants who may otherwise face barriers to international mobility.

Why it matters here: This is a live, named example of a European consortium using the same Erasmus+ KA171-HED funding line as the Wits-Aix-Marseille project to run graduate traineeships with Latin American partners, and its explicit attention to applicants facing barriers to mobility offers a concrete model the Wits project could adapt when it designs its own inclusion measures for master's students, doctoral candidates and staff travelling to Aix-Marseille.

Compostela Group of Universities (Grupo Compostela de Universidades), news item, 26 February 2026 · Institutional news article published directly by the Compostela Group of Universities, naming the funded project's reference number; read directly from the page.

entry.title: A decision-tree model flags academic risk for students in conflict-affected North Kivu (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A researcher in North Kivu, in the conflict-affected east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, built a decision-tree model in RapidMiner from academic and socio-demographic data on 350 university students to flag those at academic risk. The model reached 99.05% classification accuracy, with psychological support, grade point average, motivation level and displacement status standing out as the strongest predictors.

Why it matters here: Set in a context of displacement and disrupted study that the Wits-Emory project does not face, this case nonetheless shows the value of reaching past grades alone to socio-demographic and wellbeing indicators, exactly the kind of variable PASS could test alongside the Wits School of Education's own anonymised records once the University's Business Intelligence Services widens the data it shares.

Semajeri Ladislas Elias, International Journal of Soft Computing and Engineering (IJSCE), 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Soft Computing and Engineering), confirmed via the DOI redirect to the publisher and via the author's Zenodo-hosted record; the publisher's own page returned a 403 to automated fetching, as with other publishers checked for this feed.

entry.title: Hawaii's public university system buys predictive analytics for all ten campuses (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The University of Hawaiʻi Board of Regents approved a 7.4 million dollar, five-year subscription covering all ten UH campuses to two EAB platforms: Navigate360, which scores students' risk from indicators such as GPA, course withdrawals, advisor engagement and credit completion and sends automated alerts to faculty and advisers, and Edify, which draws academic, financial aid and student-services data into one system to remove data silos. UH President Wendy Hensel, formerly of Georgia State University, said the platforms are used at more than 850 institutions reporting graduation and retention gains of up to 15%, and that Georgia State's own four-year graduation rate rose 13% since 2012 on a model built from 2.5 million student grades.

Why it matters here: Georgia State's advising model already features in the PASS project's own case file, and Hawaii's systemwide purchase shows what buying a comparable platform at scale looks like, in cost, phased rollout and governance, as well as the biggest risk PASS should design against: most of the 'up to 15%' claim still rests on the vendor's and Georgia State's own figures rather than independent evidence from the new site, exactly the validation gap the Wits and Emory collaboration is meant to close before recommending interventions.

Maui Now, 22 June 2025, reporting the University of Hawaiʻi Board of Regents · News report of a public university system's Board of Regents decision, citing figures given by the university's own president and officials; the graduation and retention gains quoted are the vendor's and Georgia State's figures, not yet independent results from Hawaii.

entry.title: A randomised comparison finds gamified mobile teaching raises civil engineering test scores and engagement (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Harbin University of Science and Technology randomly assigned 124 civil engineering undergraduates to an experimental group taught with gamified mobile-technology teaching or a control group taught conventionally, 62 students each. Pre-test scores showed no significant difference between the two groups, but after the intervention the experimental group's test scores were significantly higher (p = 0.003), and independent-sample t-tests found significantly greater behavioural, cognitive and emotional engagement in the gamified group. Published in July 2023, slightly outside the usual three-year window but included as a well-powered randomised comparison directly relevant to the Wits project's own controlled design.

Why it matters here: This randomised, matched-group comparison of gamified against conventional teaching in a civil engineering course, with before-and-after testing, is close in design to the controlled comparison the Wits project plans for crystallography and phase transformations, and its engagement measures (behavioural, cognitive, emotional) offer a ready-made framework for the surveys and classroom observation already planned.

Pan and Mow, International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET), vol. 18, no. 14, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access, confirmed by fetching the journal's own article page.

entry.title: A blended intensive programme on multilingualism and inclusive teaching across the T4EU alliance (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski is coordinating a Blended Intensive Programme called 'Multilingualism, Inclusive Learning and Intercultural Dialogue' for the Transform4Europe (T4EU) European University Alliance. Online sessions on 21 April and 2 June 2026 bracket an on-site week in Sofia from 11 to 15 May 2026, worth 5 ECTS credits and open to students, PhD students, researchers, university teachers and administrative staff, covering multilingualism as a resource, inclusive pedagogy, intercultural communication and digital multilingual environments.

Why it matters here: CIVIS and the Wits-Aix-Marseille project could borrow this short virtual-plus-one-week format: it lets academics, doctoral candidates and administrative staff from several institutions earn credit for multilingual and inclusive teaching work without committing to a full semester abroad, which suits the project's own mix of master's students, doctoral candidates, academics and administrative staff.

Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski, T4EU announcement, 2026 · Institutional announcement on the Transform4Europe (T4EU) European University Alliance page hosted by Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski, verified by fetching the page directly; T4EU is a European Commission funded European University Alliance of universities across several countries, and the Blended Intensive Programme format itself is an Erasmus+ instrument.

entry.title: Two years of Erasmus+ KA171 mobility between a Pakistani and a Spanish university (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Two students from the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST) in Pakistan were hosted at the University of Málaga in Spain over two academic years under the Erasmus+ KA171 scheme, remotely supervised for close to a year before arrival and then completing a semester of coursework and a bachelor's thesis in a photonics research group. The paper reports long, unpredictable visa processing from Pakistan and difficulty securing housing from abroad, and it calls for more administrative support and more English-taught courses to widen the impact of such mobilities.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille project uses the same KA171 funding line, so this paper's concrete lessons on remote preparation, visa delays and housing from abroad are directly transferable to planning mobility for Wits master's students, doctoral candidates and administrative staff travelling to Aix-Marseille.

Luque-González, Sánchez-Postigo, Pérez-Galacho & González-Andrade, INTED2026 Proceedings · Peer-reviewed conference paper in the INTED2026 proceedings (20th International Technology, Education and Development Conference, Valencia, 2-4 March 2026); verified through its iated.org Digital Library record, which gives the DOI, ISBN, ISSN and abstract.

entry.title: Doubly robust evaluation finds AI-guided support reduces course failures at a New Zealand university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A December 2025 preprint by researchers at Massey University in New Zealand used propensity score matching and doubly robust treatment-effect estimation to evaluate AI-guided support for 1,859 at-risk students who received at least one intervention between 2022 and 2024. It found statistically significant reductions in courses failed (down 0.78 in the intervention year and 3.60 cumulatively) and significant increases in cumulative mean grade (up 8.82 points) and cumulative percentage of courses passed (up 13.99 percentage points), while effects on overall qualification completion remained statistically imprecise. The authors used Activity Theory to interpret the support as stabilising at-risk students' trajectories rather than necessarily accelerating their completion.

Why it matters here: This gives PASS a rigorous, borrowable method for moving beyond correlational risk-flagging to actual causal evidence of what its co-created interventions change, using propensity score matching, doubly robust estimation and a Rosenbaum sensitivity check for hidden bias. Its honest finding that completion effects remain uncertain even where failure and grade effects are significant is a useful calibration for what PASS should expect to demonstrate in its own early evaluations.

Susnjak, Bakhshov & Mathrani, arXiv preprint, 2025 · Preprint by university-affiliated researchers posted on arXiv, verified by fetching the full paper's methods and results sections directly.

entry.title: Open University builds a student-facing dashboard with predictive and prescriptive analytics (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The Open University's Institute of Educational Technology ran a Student-Facing Learning Analytics Dashboard project from September 2023 to August 2025, co-designed with 30 students and tested with over 300 students, giving each student descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics such as virtual learning environment engagement, the likelihood of passing the next assignment and recommended study materials. Using propensity score matching, the project's evaluation found that students who engaged with the dashboard achieved better course performance than those who did not. The project was funded by the Open University's Access, Participation and Success team in the Faculty of Business and Law.

Why it matters here: This shows a method PASS could borrow: propensity score matching to evaluate whether a student-facing predictive dashboard actually changes outcomes, not merely whether students use it, which is directly relevant to PASS's plan to co-create interventions with Wits University's Business Intelligence Services. It is also a precedent for moving beyond a staff-only early-alert tool to one that gives predictions and recommendations directly to students.

Institute of Educational Technology, The Open University, 2023-2025 · Official project page published by The Open University's Institute of Educational Technology, verified by fetching the page directly.

entry.title: A digital escape room built in Unreal Engine 5 to review Statics concepts (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Engineering education researchers at Ohio Northern University, USA, are building a single-player video game in Unreal Engine 5 that turns the undergraduate Statics course, which covers forces and moments on rigid bodies in equilibrium, into a three-room digital escape room. Students must solve a chandelier equilibrium puzzle, a platform traversal and a three-dimensional cable-tension problem to progress, and the paper, presented at the 2025 ASEE North Central Section Conference, sets out plans to evaluate the game through in-game completion and attempt metrics alongside pre- and post-game confidence surveys, though no outcome data are yet reported because the game is still in development.

Why it matters here: This is a discipline-specific digital escape room built to rehearse exactly the kind of equilibrium and force-balance problems that metallurgical engineering students must also master, and its planned mixed-methods evaluation, in-game analytics paired with pre- and post-game confidence surveys, closely matches the surveys, interviews and classroom observation the Wits project is already planning for its own digital games.

Seyed Ardakani and Kamatali, ASEE North Central Section Conference, 2025 · Conference paper (Work in Progress) in the ASEE PEER repository, confirmed by downloading and reading the full PDF directly from the publisher's site.

entry.title: Erasmus Mundus students and alumni report widespread visa and residence permit problems (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A survey of 325 Erasmus Mundus joint master's students and alumni, most of them from outside the European Union, was run by EMA's Policy and Quality Assurance Unit between October and December 2023 and reported in an Academic Cooperation Association newsletter. It found recurring problems with visa appointment scheduling, documentation requirements and delays, which cost respondents considerable time and money and in some cases put their academic mobility at risk, and it recommends more consistent visa procedures across European Union member states, stronger support from consortia and institutions, and consideration of a dedicated Erasmus+ mobility visa.

Why it matters here: Wits participants travelling to France under the Erasmus+ KA171 project face the same kind of visa friction this survey documents, so its findings are an equity warning for the partnership's mobility planning, and its call for a dedicated Erasmus+ visa is a concrete policy ask that CIVIS could pursue on Wits's behalf.

Academic Cooperation Association (ACA) Secretariat Newsletter, reporting the EMA Visa Experiences Survey, 2025 · Newsletter item of the Academic Cooperation Association (ACA), a Brussels-based higher education policy network, reporting a survey carried out by the Erasmus Mundus Student and Alumni Association (EMA); verified by fetching both the ACA newsletter page and the EMA survey landing page it links to.

entry.title: A survey of six gamification types and their reported effect on Cuban engineering students (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Universidad de Holguín in Cuba surveyed 575 engineering students and 70 engineering lecturers about six types of gamified strategy used in class: simulation games, competitions and challenges, interactive evaluations, collaborative projects, combined theoretical-practical gamification, and points, levels and rewards. The authors report self-assessed skill gains after gamification, for example problem-solving rising from 60% to 85% and critical thinking from 70% to 90%, and average grades rising from 65% at the start of the three-month study to 85% by its end.

Why it matters here: As a rare published gamification study from Cuba, it broadens the project's evidence base beyond the Western European and Mexican studies that dominate the literature, and its six named gamification types, each linked to a specific skill profile such as decision-making or autonomy, offer a simple framework the Wits team could test against its own board games, digital games and gamified assessment in metallurgical engineering.

Álvarez Márquez, Clavel Quintero and de Feria Hernández, Journal TechInnovation, 2024 · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article reporting a descriptive, non-experimental survey, confirmed by reading the full published PDF directly from the journal's own site.

entry.title: A simulation game framework tested against conventional teaching in civil engineering (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers from King Faisal University in Saudi Arabia and the National University of Sciences and Technology in Pakistan ran an intervention study comparing a control group taught civil engineering concepts by conventional methods with an experimental group introduced to a simulation game, then surveyed both groups on their learning experience. Independent t-tests found a higher mean score for entertainment via the game (4.13) than for traditional teaching (3.72), and 85% of students said the game helped reinforce civil engineering concepts compared with 67% for traditional methods, with many students suggesting the game be expanded to cover more topics.

Why it matters here: This controlled comparison between a simulation game and conventional teaching, using a simple survey of matched groups, offers a directly usable evaluation template for the Wits project's own comparison of gamified and conventional approaches to crystallography and phase transformations, and the students' request to expand the game to more topics speaks directly to the co-design workshops already planned at Wits.

Zubair, Khan, Hassan, Ahmed and Aziz, Sustainability (MDPI), 2024 · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article in MDPI's journal Sustainability, confirmed via the publisher's Crossref metadata record for the DOI, including the full abstract (direct access to the MDPI page itself returned a 403 to automated fetching, as with another MDPI article checked for this feed).

entry.title: Survey of five Ugandan universities finds non-academic factors outweigh academic ones in student dropout (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A 2024 study in The Uganda Higher Education Review surveyed 532 continuing and final-year students, validated on a sample of 523, across five private and government universities in central Uganda, using the design science research method and a questionnaire with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.821. It found non-academic factors accounted for 60% of reported dropout drivers against 40% for academic factors, with social factors (21.6%), work (16.5%) and the lack of a free or reduced lunch programme (18.8%) among the largest single contributors, and proposed, but explicitly described as not yet validated, a machine learning early-warning algorithm drawing on academic performance, marital status, fee-payment status and family background.

Why it matters here: This is a useful contrast for PASS: evidence from five Ugandan universities that non-academic and financial factors, such as fees, family circumstances and work, can outweigh academic performance in explaining dropout, a reminder to test social and financial variables alongside academic ones in the Wits School of Education data. Its candid description of its own predictive algorithm as unvalidated work in progress is also a useful precedent for staging PASS's model development and validation transparently.

Mukooyo & Kasse, The Uganda Higher Education Review, 2024 · Peer-reviewed article in The Uganda Higher Education Review, the journal of Uganda's National Council for Higher Education, verified by downloading and reading the complete published PDF.

entry.title: University of Da Nang joins an Erasmus+ KA171 capacity-building week in Portugal, the only Vietnamese institution present (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A delegation from the University of Da Nang took part in International Week at the Polytechnic Institute of Cávado and Ave (IPCA) in Portugal from 11 to 15 May 2026, under the Erasmus+ KA171 project, alongside representatives from more than 20 countries; the university's own account describes it as the only Vietnamese institution present. The week combined an academic forum at which institutions presented their strengths with capacity-building sessions on selecting and developing partners for European-funded projects and on writing Erasmus+ KA2 proposals, and a working session with IPCA's leadership on possible areas of cooperation; no agreement or specific partnership decision was announced.

Why it matters here: Da Nang's capacity-building sessions on choosing partners and writing proposals for European-funded projects are exactly the practical skills Wits International and the Wits School of Education need to carry the Aix-Marseille partnership past its first KA171 grant into a renewed or a KA2 scheme, and Da Nang's position as sole representative of its country is a caution the Wits-Aix-Marseille team can use to argue for building a wider Southern African cohort around the partnership rather than relying on one university alone.

University of Da Nang, May 2026 · Official news page of the University of Da Nang, naming the host institution, the dates and the delegation

entry.title: Random forest outperforms seven other models in predicting undergraduate dropout at a Thai university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Rajamangala University of Technology Suvarnabhumi compared eight machine learning models on records of 2,104 science and technology undergraduates from 2020 to 2024, using 36 data features, k-nearest-neighbour imputation for missing values and SMOTE to correct class imbalance. Random forest performed best, reaching 84.32 per cent accuracy with a precision of 0.85, a recall of 0.84 and an F1 score of 0.85.

Why it matters here: PASS is testing several model families on Wits School of Education data; this head-to-head comparison across eight algorithms on a comparably sized dataset, with random forest beating the rest, gives PASS a concrete benchmark model and preprocessing recipe (imputation plus SMOTE) to trial against its own candidates.

Satmunee, Naowanich & Patikorn, Journal of Science and Technology Mahasarakham University, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Journal of Science and Technology Mahasarakham University, Thai Journal Citation Index Tier 1), confirmed by fetching the journal's own article page

entry.title: Five factors explain seven in ten cases of retention risk among distance-learning students at an Indonesian open university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universitas Terbuka, Indonesia's open university, surveyed 200 active distance-learning students identified as at risk of academic withdrawal at its Makassar regional office, and used multiple linear regression to test five groups of factors against retention. Academic, social, institutional, motivational and external factors together were statistically significant (p < 0.05) and accounted for an adjusted 70.4 per cent of the variation in retention, though the paper does not report which single factor mattered most.

Why it matters here: PASS also starts from students already flagged as at risk, but builds a predictive score rather than a factor survey; this study's finding that five broad, measurable factor groups explain most of the variation in retention is a useful check for which categories of variable PASS should make sure its own administrative data cover, especially non-academic ones such as motivation and external circumstances.

Jamil, Halim, Hasan, Lince & Tahir, Proceeding of the International Conference on Innovation in Open and Distance Learning (INNODEL), 2025 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings paper (INNODEL, Universitas Terbuka), confirmed by fetching the conference's own article page

entry.title: A SEFI workshop teaches engineering lecturers to build AI-supported escape room tasks for engineering mathematics (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
At the 53rd SEFI Annual Conference in Tampere in September 2025, Rasteiro, Suleiman and Kaneko ran a hands-on workshop teaching engineering lecturers to design escape room tasks for mathematics using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. Participants used the tools to build puzzles set in real engineering scenarios, connecting abstract mathematical concepts to practice, and left with classroom-ready materials, worked examples and prompt-engineering guidance for their own courses.

Why it matters here: This is a direct, very recent example of lecturers themselves using generative AI to design the kind of puzzle-based, game-like assessment the Wits gamification project is exploring for metallurgical engineering, offering a template, a prompt-engineering guide and a peer network the project's own board-game and digital-game design workshops could draw on.

Rasteiro, Suleiman and Kaneko, 53rd SEFI Annual Conference, Tampere, 2025 · Conference proceedings record of the 53rd SEFI Annual Conference, held at Tampere University, confirmed by fetching the repository listing; the full workshop paper itself was not available for fetch

entry.title: An early-warning model built only from pre-enrolment data flags three in five incoming students at a Mexican university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Instituto Tecnológico de Sonora in Mexico built an XGBoost classifier trained only on data available at the moment of enrolment, using a retrospective dataset of almost 40,000 first-year students from 2014 to 2024. The model reached an AUC-ROC of 0.69 and an F1 score of 0.69 for the dropout class, with 88 per cent sensitivity, and flagged 59 per cent of incoming students as high risk, with considerable variation across academic programmes. Age, high school grade point average, conditioned admission, family responsibilities and economic constraints were the most influential predictors.

Why it matters here: PASS is likewise built from a new entering cohort's administrative data; ITSON's choice to use only pre-enrolment variables, so that every incoming student can be scored before teaching even starts, is a direct design option for how early PASS could flag Wits School of Education entrants, and its finding that risk varies sharply by programme is a caution for how PASS reports results across departments.

Carballo-Mendívil, Arellano-González, Ríos-Vázquez & Lizardi-Duarte, Applied Sciences, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Applied Sciences, MDPI); confirmed from the Crossref and OpenAlex metadata records after the publisher's own page returned an access-denied error to automated fetch

entry.title: Five Jamaican students win fully funded Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters scholarships (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Five Jamaican students, four of them graduates of the University of the West Indies and one of the University of Florida, were awarded fully funded Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters scholarships for study beginning in the 2025 to 2026 academic year, the European Union's delegation in Kingston announced on 14 August 2025. The scholarships cover tuition, travel and a living allowance for one to two years of study across at least three European countries in fields including islands and sustainability, cultural heritage management, coastal hazards and climate adaptation, and children's literature; the awardees will study in the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom and graduate with joint, double or multiple degrees.

Why it matters here: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters, funded under the same Erasmus+ programme as the Aix-Marseille to Wits KA171 partnership, shows a small island developing state recruiting into the consortium model that KA171 itself uses for individual mobility, evidence of the pipeline the Wits-Aix-Marseille partnership is joining and a reminder that Caribbean partners are a live comparator region for Africa's own Erasmus+ engagement.

Delegation of the European Union to Jamaica, 14 August 2025 · Official statement of the Delegation of the European Union to Jamaica, Belize, The Bahamas, Turks and Caicos Islands and Cayman Islands

entry.title: Thirty-three Nepali students awarded Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's scholarships (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The European Union awarded fully funded, two-year Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's Degree scholarships to 33 Nepali students, 17 women and 16 men, for study beginning in the 2025 to 2026 academic year across multiple European universities in fields including cybersecurity, engineering, agriculture, biology, flood risk management and food technology, the EU delegation in Kathmandu announced on 17 July 2025. The scholarships cover tuition, airfare and a monthly stipend; the delegation said more than 800 Nepali students have received Erasmus+ scholarships in total, and it held a pre-departure orientation for the new cohort on 16 July with the Erasmus Mundus Association Nepal.

Why it matters here: Nepal's run of consecutive Erasmus Mundus cohorts and its own alumni association show what a mature, long-running Erasmus+ pipeline into Europe looks like after many years, a scale and continuity that the newly selected Aix-Marseille to Wits KA171 partnership can treat as a marker of where sustained mobility funding could eventually lead if the partnership is renewed beyond its first 36 months.

Delegation of the European Union to Nepal, 17 July 2025 · Official statement of the Delegation of the European Union to Nepal

entry.title: Welten der Werkstoffe: a point-and-click adventure carries materials science students through ten parallel dimensions (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
TH Köln's Cologne Game Lab built Welten der Werkstoffe (Worlds of Materials) with Professor Martin Bonnet of the Institute for Applied Materials, as the third module of his flipped-classroom teaching concept alongside his YouTube lectures and in-class exercises. Released in April 2021, the free point-and-click adventure follows the ten chapters of his materials science lecture series, covering atomic structures, the iron-carbon diagram, steels and non-metals, aimed at Bloom's levels of application and analysis; TH Köln students taking the Materials Science elective can earn exam bonus points for playing it.

Why it matters here: Welten der Werkstoffe is a direct model for the kind of digital game the Wits gamification project is assessing: a narrative adventure built from a real materials science syllabus, with its own iron-carbon diagram chapter sitting alongside crystallography and phase transformations, and tied to course credit, giving the project a concrete design and incentive structure to compare against its own board games and digital games.

Cologne Game Lab and Professor Martin Bonnet, TH Köln, released April 2021 · Institutional project page of TH Köln's Cologne Game Lab, confirmed by fetching the page itself

entry.title: A three-dimensional Bloom's taxonomy matrix measures what gamified training teaches at the Stellenbosch Learning Factory (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Stellenbosch University's Department of Industrial Engineering set up the Stellenbosch Learning Factory to help address South Africa's skills shortage at tertiary level, using experiential, production-like 'learning by doing'. Henning, Hagedorn-Hansen and Von Leipzig (2017) studied what the Learning Factory's games contribute to learning by building a three-dimensional matrix based on a revised Bloom's taxonomy to assess the games' learning success.

Why it matters here: The Learning Factory shows a South African engineering faculty using games specifically to close a skills gap and measuring the result with a structured taxonomy rather than survey impressions alone, a method the Wits gamification project can draw on when it designs its own assessment of what its board games and digital games actually teach metallurgy students, not just how much students enjoy them.

Henning, Hagedorn-Hansen and Von Leipzig, South African Journal of Industrial Engineering, 2017 · Peer-reviewed journal article, South African Journal of Industrial Engineering (open access); confirmed from the published abstract and the Stellenbosch University repository record, the full-text PDF could not be parsed by automated fetch

entry.title: A tower-building game scores civil engineering graduate attributes at three stages of a Costa Rican degree (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Costa Rica's Civil Engineering School designed a game-based tower-construction activity and ran it with 28 student teams, more than 110 students in all, at the initial, intermediate and advanced stages of the Civil Engineering programme. Observable performance indicators, normalised against each cohort, produced comparable scores out of 100 across five accreditation graduate attributes. Design and development, environment and sustainability, and teamwork improved significantly across the three stages, problem analysis stayed stable, and project administration and finances rose gradually; a student survey rated the activity's clarity and fairness highly.

Why it matters here: The Wits gamification project is itself testing whether games can generate credible evidence of learning and not only engagement; this Costa Rican methodology, scoring graduate attributes from a tower-building game at successive stages of a degree, offers a concrete model for turning board or digital games in metallurgical engineering into evidence a programme can use for accreditation, not only for teaching.

Mata Abdelnour et al., Quality Assurance in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, advance online publication, Quality Assurance in Education

entry.title: African scientists propose an Erasmus-style mobility scheme to tackle the continent's brain drain (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
At a panel hosted by the Embassy of Tunisia on inter-African cooperation at Science Forum South Africa 2025, held at the CSIR in Pretoria, government, academic and industry participants called for an Erasmus-style continental qualification and mobility scheme to counter the loss of scientific talent to developed nations. Their proposals included expanded scholarships, joint PhD initiatives, cross-border research partnerships, harmonised qualification frameworks and streamlined visa systems, alongside a suggestion to teach Swahili from early childhood as a unifying continental language. Panellists named political will, sustainable funding and institutional capacity for cross-border qualification recognition as the main obstacles to implementation.

Why it matters here: The panel is calling, continent-wide, for the kind of staff and student mobility, joint degree work and streamlined recognition that the Wits-Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ KA171 project is already running between two institutions; it is a reminder that the project's own visa, funding and qualification-recognition arrangements are being watched as a working example of what a continental scheme would need to get right.

Smith, Mail & Guardian, 2025 · News report on a Science Forum South Africa panel, a government- and industry-attended policy forum held at the CSIR in Pretoria

entry.title: Short overseas placements build caring and practical skills faster than deep subject knowledge for Taiwanese trainee teachers (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A qualitative study of preservice teachers from National Pingtung University in Taiwan who taught at partner primary schools in Kampar, Malaysia, under a short-term international mobility programme found that the brief placement limited how far participants deepened subject-specific teaching knowledge, but it noticeably strengthened their exploratory, practical and caring competencies. Drawing on interviews, reflective reports and teaching documentation, the authors report that participants, especially those abroad for the first time, became more attentive to cross-cultural classroom contexts, reflected more on their own teaching and showed greater concern for educational equity and social justice.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange is itself a short-term mobility scheme for teacher-education students and staff; this study is direct evidence that even a brief overseas placement reliably builds intercultural and reflective competence, while warning the project not to expect the same placements to deepen subject-specific teaching knowledge without a longer stay or follow-up support.

Lin, Lin & Lee, Journal of International Students, 2025 · Peer-reviewed qualitative study, open access

entry.title: A Vietnamese university compares three machine-learning models for predicting student dropout on an international benchmark dataset (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A researcher at Thuy Loi University in Hanoi compared a neural network, a random forest and a support vector machine on a widely used international benchmark dataset of 4,424 student records with 36 features covering the first two years of academic results and social factors, after rebalancing the dropout and graduate classes. Random forest performed best, reaching 91.33% accuracy. The paper states that this is the first Vietnamese study to apply these methods to dropout prediction, but notes that the benchmark dataset itself holds no Vietnamese student records, and recommends adding local data and re-weighting features before the model is applied to Vietnamese students.

Why it matters here: PASS likewise starts, by design, with a smaller first dataset, anonymised Wits School of Education records, before any wider rollout, so this paper's own caution, that a model built on one population's data needs local data and re-weighted features before it is trusted elsewhere, is a direct question for how PASS plans to extend its model beyond its first cohort.

Hoa, TNU Journal of Science and Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed article in a Vietnamese university's bilingual science journal, published with a DOI; fetched and read in full

entry.title: An open-source quest system helps students take their first steps contributing to open source software (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Northern Arizona University and Oregon State University in the United States, with the Federal Technological University of Parana (UTFPR) in Brazil, built OSSDoorway, a gamified, quest-based environment that scaffolds students through the steps of contributing to a real open-source software project, including using GitHub features to submit pull requests. The team recruited 29 students, gave them a self-efficacy questionnaire before and after they used the tool, and collected qualitative feedback on its challenges and interface. Students' self-efficacy increased after using OSSDoorway, and the authors report that clear instructions, real-time feedback and the quest structure helped students navigate the open-source contribution process and collaborate with the wider community.

Why it matters here: Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering shares OSSDoorway's central question, whether structured quests and real-time feedback can lift a student's confidence to attempt an unfamiliar, real-world task; the self-efficacy questionnaire the authors used is itself a transferable instrument the Wits project could adapt alongside its own surveys, interviews and co-design workshops on crystallography and phase-transformation games.

Santos et al., arXiv preprint, 2025 · Preprint on arXiv (cs.SE / cs.HC); independent confirmation of peer-reviewed conference or journal publication not found

entry.title: A review of nine bilingual education programmes across six Francophone West African countries finds teacher training in the mother tongue is what makes them work (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A review of nine bilingual or mother-tongue education programmes in Niger, Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire and Cameroon found mixed results that tracked closely with whether teachers were trained and resourced to teach in the mother tongue rather than only in French. Burkina Faso's Programme d'éducation bilingue, which trained teachers in the mother tongue, produced higher pass rates and lower repetition; Mali's Pédagogie Convergente gave teachers materials in both languages and improved French and maths scores; but in Côte d'Ivoire, where teachers lacked mother-tongue materials and training, bilingual-school pupils read and spoke worse than their French-only peers.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille project trains bilingual teaching specifically, so this review is a direct, comparative evidence base on the single factor it identifies as decisive, whether teachers themselves are trained and resourced in the second language of instruction, and a caution that mobility or exchange without that training will not close the gap it is meant to close.

Ball, Bhattacharya, Zhao, Akpé, Brogno & Jasińska, International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism, 2024 · Peer-reviewed review article

entry.title: Faster is not always right: a Japanese study checks the speed-accuracy trade-off in gamified Kahoot quizzes (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A brief research report from Kyoto University of Advanced Science analysed 4,640 response-time and accuracy records from 98 first-year engineering students, 46 Japanese and 52 international, across 21 Kahoot quiz modules run in an Android app development course in 2022 and 2023. In 17 of the 21 modules, wrong answers took significantly longer than correct ones, and response time correlated negatively with accuracy in 13 modules, running counter to the classic speed-accuracy trade-off seen in untimed tasks. The author attributes this to the quiz's per-question time limit and a scoring system that rewards fast correct answers, and notes that question difficulty and topic changed the pattern.

Why it matters here: Engineering education in an AI-mediated world is turning to tools such as Kahoot for gamified assessment, which the metallurgical engineering project is itself weighing; this study is a caution that a timed quiz or leaderboard can reward speed over understanding, a design question worth testing before timing becomes part of any crystallography or phase-transformation quiz.

Liang, Frontiers in Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed brief research report, open access, Frontiers in Education

entry.title: A conceptual framework traces Wits' own 2015 big data early-alert project to propose one model for South African universities (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Writing from the University of Zululand, N. Cele draws on action research at two South African universities, the biographic data collection system the University of the Witwatersrand introduced at first-time registration in 2015, and a similar tool the University of Zululand introduced in 2018, to argue that early-alert systems need an integrated biographic, socio-economic and academic profile of each student, not academic records alone. The article proposes a big data integration framework for student profiling and performance tracking, and concludes that collecting such biographic information is what lets a university tell whether a student's difficulties stem from a privileged or a disenfranchised background, so that support can be designed accordingly.

Why it matters here: The 2015 Wits project this article is built on is the same institution, and close to the same biographic data, that PASS now draws on at the School of Education, making it the direct conceptual ancestor of PASS' own model; its argument, that an early-alert score means little without the biographic and socio-economic profile behind it, is a first test for whichever variables PASS chooses to build its own risk score from.

Cele, South African Journal of Higher Education, 2021 · Peer-reviewed conceptual article in an accredited South African journal; fetched and read in full

entry.title: Mohawk College builds an early predictive model for incoming students at risk of leaving (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Mohawk College and the Education Policy Research Initiative built a predictive model from administrative records of students who had entered the college between 2005 and 2012, then used it to forecast the risk of early departure for students entering in Fall 2013 and 2014, sorting them into high, medium and low risk groups. The predicted leaving rates closely matched the rates actually observed. Female students, older students and those in graduate certificate programmes had lower rates of leaving early, and, against the researchers' expectations, students in the high and medium risk groups took up the college's advising programmes at higher rates than low risk students.

Why it matters here: PASS is building the same kind of model, a predictive risk score from historical administrative data applied to a new entering cohort, so Mohawk's finding, that a correct risk score does not by itself guarantee the right students take up support, is a direct caution for how PASS designs its own hand off of flagged students to Wits' Business Intelligence Services.

Finnie, Fricker, Bozkurt, Poirier & Pavlic, Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario, 2017 · Institutional research report published by the Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario, an agency of the Government of Ontario; the PDF itself could not be parsed by automated fetch, so this entry is confirmed from HEQCO's own landing page, which names the report, its authors and date and quotes its findings in full

entry.title: An Ethiopian send-off for 55 new Erasmus Mundus scholars shows how pre-departure support works at scale (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The EU Delegation to Ethiopia announced that 55 Ethiopian students received Erasmus+ scholarships for the 2025-2026 academic year to pursue Erasmus Mundus joint master's degrees across university consortia in 12 European countries. At a pre-departure event on 28 July 2026 at the EU Delegation's office in Addis Ababa, attended by EU Deputy Head of Mission Agnieszka Karpinska and member-state embassy representatives, the new scholars received guidance on travel, visas, and studying and living in Europe, and met other Erasmus Mundus alumni. The Delegation said more than 600 Ethiopian students have received fully funded Erasmus scholarships since 2010.

Why it matters here: This shows the scale Erasmus+ scholarship mobility can reach from a single African country and a practical model for supporting outgoing cohorts, a structured pre-departure briefing on visas, travel and life in Europe, paired with a standing alumni network, that the smaller, bilateral Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project could adapt for its own outgoing master's, doctoral and staff cohorts.

The Brussels Times, 3 August 2026 · News report citing the EU Delegation's own announcement

entry.title: Five Kenyan universities open a managed "academic corridor" to Romania built on Erasmus+ mobility (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Five Kenyan universities, Kabarak, Amref International, Strathmore, Moi and Pwani, signed agreements from 25 to 28 May 2026 with Romania's Danubius International University to open what organisers called East Africa's first fully managed Kenya-Romania academic corridor, facilitated by the Kenyan firm AspiraPath LLC. The corridor offers structured pathways to EU-accredited degrees through joint degree programmes, Erasmus+ mobility frameworks and joint research supervision, letting students complete part of their training locally, and organisers said it aims to reduce the tuition costs, visa difficulties and fragmented partnerships that otherwise limit access to European higher education.

Why it matters here: This is a non-governmental, facilitator-built alternative to a bilateral KA171 project, built explicitly to solve the same access barriers, cost, visas and fragmented links, that Wits-Aix-Marseille's own mobility is designed to address through direct EU funding; it is a useful contrast for the project to watch, since it shows a private, fee-based corridor model competing for the same students a publicly funded exchange like KA171 is meant to serve.

The Standard (Kenya), 25 May 2026 · News report, corroborated by a second Kenyan outlet (The Star)

entry.title: A free synthetic dataset lets researchers build and test early-warning student-success models without touching real records (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
SynEdu-HEDL is a fully synthetic dataset released on Zenodo in March 2026 by Sanjay Agal of Parul University, built to support privacy-preserving research in learning analytics and educational data mining. It imitates realistic student behaviour, performance and digital engagement across six interconnected tables covering student profiles, course metadata, learning-management-system logs, assessments, engagement metrics and outcome labels. It is released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence and is intended for building and benchmarking machine-learning models that predict at-risk students, dropout risk and learning gains.

Why it matters here: Before any model trained on Wits School of Education data is shared more widely, PASS could build a synthetic dataset the same way as SynEdu-HEDL, imitating real engagement and outcome patterns without exposing real student records, so collaborators and reviewers can test the pipeline and the project can demonstrate its methods openly.

Agal, Zenodo, 2026 · Open dataset repository (Zenodo), Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, verified by direct read of the record

entry.title: A University of South Africa review of a decade of research sets out how to govern AI-driven learning analytics fairly (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A narrative review by two University of South Africa academics synthesises research published between 2015 and 2025 on how AI-driven learning analytics in higher education link student engagement data to measurable academic outcomes, with particular attention to the South African context. It traces a shift from traditional dashboards toward deep-learning and transformer-based systems that combine behavioural, cognitive and affective indicators, and identifies data fragmentation, algorithmic opacity and limited contextual adaptation as the main obstacles. Grounded in UNESCO and OECD guidance and South Africa's Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA), the review sets out a governance-driven approach, arguing that sustainable adoption needs human-centred ethics, robust data governance and context-sensitive innovation.

Why it matters here: PASS is itself an AI-driven predictive model being built on South African higher-education data, so this review's governance checklist, data fragmentation, algorithmic opacity, contextual adaptation and POPIA compliance, is a direct list of questions for the project to put to its own data pipeline and any future dashboard before results reach the School of Education or Wits' Business Intelligence Services.

Ajayi & Letseka, Trends in Higher Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed narrative review in an open-access journal; full text blocked to automated fetch (HTTP 403), so this entry is drawn from the publisher-deposited abstract and metadata, verified via Crossref and Semantic Scholar

entry.title: A story-driven online gamification strategy for a university chemistry course for non-chemistry majors in Argentina (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universidad Tecnologica Nacional in Argentina and the Universitat de Lleida in Spain designed and evaluated Aventura Quimica, an online teaching strategy that threads a specially written story through a university chemistry course for students who are not chemistry majors. The study combined two student questionnaires with data drawn from the course's virtual learning environment. The authors report a positive student reception and describe the strategy as useful and transferable to other teaching settings.

Why it matters here: Aventura Quimica gives the Wits gamification team a worked example of a narrative-driven gamification strategy for a compulsory, non-major science course at a technological university, the same setting as metallurgical engineering students taking chemistry and materials courses, and a method, a course-long story paired with virtual-learning-environment analytics, that could be adapted for crystallography or phase-transformation content.

Boglione and Marin, Educacion Quimica, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Educacion Quimica, UNAM); the publisher's own page blocks automated access (Cloudflare bot protection), verified instead via the Universitat de Lleida institutional repository record and the DOI redirect

entry.title: A chronological catalogue of 25 years of serious games built to teach software engineering, published as an open dataset (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Castilla-La Mancha and the University of Murcia published a catalogue, as a dataset on Zenodo, of serious games built to teach software engineering concepts from 1999 to August 2024, arranged in chronological order. Each entry gives a brief description and either a link to the game or the creator's contact details where no link survives. The dataset carries a CC BY 4.0 licence and was produced under the OASSIS-UMU project, funded by Spain's state research agency.

Why it matters here: This gives the Wits gamification team a ready-made, citable map of a quarter-century of serious games in one engineering discipline, a model worth copying for a similar catalogue of the board games, digital games and escape rooms already gathered for metallurgical and materials engineering, and a reminder that cataloguing existing games, not only building new ones, is itself a useful contribution to the field.

Vizcaino, Fernandez-Aleman and Casas, Zenodo, 2025 · Open dataset on Zenodo, CC BY 4.0 licence, produced under a state-funded research project

entry.title: A 360-degree browser puzzle game introduces prospective materials-science students to shape-memory alloys at TU Darmstadt (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
TU Darmstadt published Mission Metal Memory, the first game in its TUDa Campus Quest series: a puzzle-based serious game set in a 360-degree virtual replica of its campus, in which a prospective student finds the lecture hall, follows a short lecture on shape-memory alloys, runs a virtual lab experiment and completes a quiz in place of writing a lab protocol. It was built by the university's E-Learning working group with content from its Institute of Materials Science, within the Future Learning Spaces project, and is free to play in a browser. The university states that further Campus Quest games, for mechanical engineering, civil engineering and architecture, are in development.

Why it matters here: Mission Metal Memory shows how a short, browser-based serious game about shape-memory alloys and laboratory protocol can carry real materials-science content for an audience outside the classroom, a model the Wits gamification project could adapt as an orientation or outreach game that previews crystallography or phase-transformation topics before students meet them in the metallurgical engineering curriculum.

Bischler, TU Darmstadt news, 2024 · Institutional news and programme page (TU Darmstadt)

entry.title: A Nordic study finds European partners kept more say over who joins student-teacher mobility to Africa (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A peer-reviewed study in Nordisk tidsskrift for pedagogikk og kritikk interviewed four facilitators of Norwegian student teachers' mobility in Tanzania and Zambia and three teacher educators in Norway, to examine how (de)colonial dynamics shape this south-bound mobility. It found that facilitators from Norway, the Global North partner, had more freedom to shape mobility activities, including the freedom to choose partner institutions, reproducing asymmetrical power relations through the mobility itself. The authors argue Norwegian teacher education still needs decolonial theoretical frameworks to recognise and address this imbalance.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project moves people in both directions, but this study is a direct warning for any two-way scheme: unless partner choice and activity design are genuinely shared, the European side can end up with more control even when the mobility itself flows south as well as north. It is a check the project's own governance and staff-mobility planning can be measured against.

Massao, P. B. & Bergersen, A., Nordisk tidsskrift for pedagogikk og kritikk, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Marist College's open-source MUSE dashboard turns nightly data feeds into a faculty-facing risk score for every student (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Marist College's Data Science and Analytics Department rolled out MUSE (Marist Universal Student Experience) in 2018, an early-alert dashboard built into the college's Sakai-based learning management system that gives faculty a visual risk status for each student in their class.
